title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words
summary: Clarifies that the key words in RFC 2119 only have their special meaning when written in uppercase. Lowercase uses are ordinary English. It updates RFC 2119 and is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2119 defines words like MUST and MAY with precise meanings in IETF specifications. RFC 8174 clarifies that only the all-capital forms carry those meanings. Lowercase 'must' and 'should' keep their normal English sense.

questions: what does uppercase must mean in an rfc
subtitle: A short fix that says only ALL-CAPS MUST and SHOULD carry the special RFC 2119 meanings.

tldr.problem: RFC 2119 said its key words are 'often capitalized', which left readers unsure how to treat lowercase 'must' and 'should'.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8174 replaces one paragraph of RFC 2119 so the key words have their defined meanings only when written in all capitals; in lowercase they are ordinary English.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 2119 and supplies new boilerplate that cites BCP 14 and applies only when the words appear in all capitals.

today: RFC 8174 is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 2119. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Ambiguity
sections.content: RFC 2119 specifies common key words, such as MUST, SHOULD and MAY, that may be used in protocol specifications. It says the words 'are often capitalized', which caused confusion about how to interpret non-capitalized words such as 'must' and 'should'. RFC 8174 updates RFC 2119 to settle the question, and it is part of BCP 14.
sections.plainLanguage: A rulebook said the special words were 'often' in capitals, so readers could not tell whether small-letter versions counted. This RFC answers that question.

sections.title: What RFC 2119 Now Says
sections.content: The RFC replaces an old paragraph of RFC 2119 with a new one. The new text makes three points. The words can be used as defined, but using them is not required: normative text does not need the key words, and a lot of normative text does not use them and is still normative. The words have the meanings RFC 2119 specifies only when they are in all capitals. When they are not capitalized, they have their normal English meanings and are not affected by the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Caps MUST carries the defined requirement level. Lowercase must is just a normal English word and the rules of this document do not apply to it.

sections.title: The Updated Boilerplate
sections.content: Authors who follow the guidelines should place a phrase near the beginning of their document. The new phrase lists the key words, now adding NOT RECOMMENDED, and says they are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 (RFC 2119 and RFC 8174) 'when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here'.
sections.plainLanguage: Specifications include one sentence that says the all-capital words are the special ones, and that the special meanings apply only to them.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content: The document requires no IANA actions. It describes itself as purely procedural and states that there are no related security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC only changes how a rule is written down, so it creates no new security risk.

references.text: Bradner, S., "Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels", BCP 14, RFC 2119, March 1997.
